in_context.text: This verse closes a short section on choosing church leaders. Paul tells Timothy not to lay hands on anyone in haste (5:22), because some people's sins are plain at once while others come out later (5:24). Verse 25 says the same about good works: some are obvious now, and the rest cannot stay hidden.

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself as the writer of the letter.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, whom Paul had left to lead the church at Ephesus.

affected.text: The people Timothy might appoint or judge, especially elders. Their sins and good deeds will both come to light in time.

what.text: Some people's good works are plain to see from the start. The good works that are not obvious yet cannot be hidden forever. So Timothy should take time before judging a person's character.

events.text: Paul writes while Timothy is leading the church at Ephesus, after Paul left for Macedonia. The church faced false teaching from within.

written.text: Traditional: about AD 62-64, by Paul. Scholarly: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110 and see it as written in Paul's name by a follower; others defend Paul's authorship and the earlier date.

where.text: The letter was sent to Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia. Where Paul wrote from is not stated; it may have been Macedonia.

purpose.text: Paul is guarding Timothy against hasty choices of leaders. Since both sin and goodness show up over time, patience leads to fairer judgment.

big_picture.text: The letter teaches that leaders must be people of proven character, and that belief and behavior belong together. This verse adds that a person's real character eventually becomes visible.

for_readers.text: Readers can take comfort that quiet good deeds are not lost. Scripture elsewhere says God sees what is done in secret and that the upright will be made known.

why_it_matters.text: The Greek word means evident beforehand or clearly evident. Some good works are obvious right away, which links this verse to the sins 'open beforehand' in 5:24.
The word means otherwise. Readers take "they that are otherwise" either as good works not yet obvious or as works that are not good; either way, they "cannot be hid."
The word means to hide or conceal. Paul says such works are not able to stay concealed, so a careful leader can expect the truth about someone to appear.

takeaway.text: Do not judge people in a hurry. In time, both the wrong and the good in a person come into the open.

resolved.reason: The cited sources don't settle what 'they that are otherwise' refers to. The lexicon gives only 'otherwise', and the phrase can mean good works not yet obvious or works that are not good. The claim flatly rules out the second reading and presents one interpretation as the only one.
resolved.fix: claim rewritten to match its sources
